core_intuitions: A checkpoint becomes a result only when paired with a defensible number AND an honest statement of what the model cannot do; the chapter has two halves in one spirit: measure honestly, then serve efficiently.

Perplexity is an effective branching factor / average surprise over held-out text; it is the one trustworthy number because it is cheap to make honest (provable exclusion), but it averages over everything and can stay flat while a narrow capability collapses.

The four measurements probe DIFFERENT skills — perplexity (predictive fit), arithmetic (reliable reasoning / RLVR check), cloze-scored MC (parametric world knowledge, near chance), retrieval-QA (reading comprehension when the answer is in context) — and the asymmetry between them IS the finding.

RTN quantization maps real-valued weights in a group onto a small integer grid via a scale (and, when asymmetric, a zero-point), rounds to nearest, clips, then dequantizes — leaving a per-weight rounding error, and treating every weight as equally important.

GPTQ and AWQ beat RTN by exploiting that some weights matter more than others: GPTQ corrects error AFTER quantizing a column by redistributing it onto not-yet-quantized columns via the Hessian; AWQ protects salient high-activation channels BEFORE quantizing by rescaling.

The storage payoff compounds: fp32->bf16->int8->int4 shrinks 406MB to ~63MB, int4 packs two nibbles per byte and pays a real scale/zero-point overhead; but int4 memory does NOT equal int4 speed because the reference path dequantizes to fp32 before the matmul.

new_figures.name: rtn-quantization-number-line
new_figures.concept: How round-to-nearest maps a group of real weights onto an integer grid via scale (symmetric) or scale+zero-point (asymmetric), then dequantizes with residual error.
new_figures.rationale: RTN is the fully-implemented reference path of the whole serving half, and every later idea (GPTQ error correction, AWQ salient-channel protection, the memory budget, int4 packing) is a delta on top of this one mapping. Readers must SEE the continuous weights snapping to a coarse grid and the rounding gap that remains — the equations in 5.1 state it but a number line makes the scale, the clip, and the per-weight error instantly legible.
new_figures.brief: A two-row diagram contrasting SYMMETRIC (top) and ASYMMETRIC (bottom) round-to-nearest for one group of weights. TOP row (symmetric, e.g. 3-bit shown for legibility so the grid isn't cramped): a horizontal number line centered on 0, spanning from -max|w| to +max|w|. Scatter ~7 small tick-marked real weight values as filled dots at irregular real positions along the line (a few clustered near zero, one near the positive extreme labeled the outlier that sets the scale). Above the line, evenly spaced vertical grid lines at the representable integer levels -(2^(b-1)-1) .. +(2^(b-1)-1), i.e. the quantization grid; label the grid spacing as 's = max|w| / (2^(b-1)-1)'. Draw short curved snap arrows from each real dot to its nearest grid line, and shade the small horizontal residual gap between original and snapped position as 'quantization error'. Mark the clip at the extreme grid line. BOTTOM row (asymmetric): same idea but the number line runs from min(w) to max(w) (NOT centered on zero — show the weights skewed positive to motivate why), grid runs 0..2^b-1, annotate the zero-point z as the integer grid index that maps back to real value 0 (draw a labeled marker where q=z lands on the real axis), and label 's = (max-min)/(2^b-1)'. A compact caption strip: 'symmetric wastes half the codes on a skewed group; asymmetric uses the full 0..2^b-1 range.' Keep to small illustrative integers only, invent no benchmark numbers. Both rows must be legible in light and dark themes — use theme-neutral strokes/fills, no hardcoded brand colors. Everything inside the viewBox, clear left-to-right reading order.
new_figures.theme_note: no hardcoded primary colors; use currentColor-style neutrals and one accent role for 'error gap'

new_figures.name: quant-memory-ladder-and-packing
new_figures.concept: The compounding storage shrink fp32->bf16->int8->int4 for Stack-100M, with the int4 two-nibbles-per-byte packing and the honest scale/zero-point overhead, and the caveat that memory shrink is not compute speedup.
new_figures.rationale: This is the chapter's headline payoff ('the whole model smaller than a folder of photos, runs on a Raspberry Pi'). The 406->203->102->63 MB ladder and the reason int4 isn't simply half of int8 (the fp32 scale/zero-point overhead) are exactly the kind of thing a proportional bar chart plus a packing inset makes visceral in a way the table cannot. The nibble-packing detail is also a concrete mechanic readers otherwise skim past.
new_figures.placement: 6. Implementing int8 and int4 Weight-Only Quantization
new_figures.brief: Left 60%: four horizontal bars stacked, one per format, widths PROPORTIONAL to total size — fp32 (~406MB, full width, labeled 1.0x), bf16 (~203MB, 2.0x), int8 row-wise (~102MB, 4.0x), int4 group=64 (~63MB, 6.4x). Each bar split into two visually distinct segments: the packed weight bytes (large) and the scale/zero-point overhead (small, only meaningfully visible on int4 where it is ~12.7MB of ~63MB — label it 'fp32 scale + zero-point per group, the part production formats compress'). Annotate each bar with its MB and the x-factor vs fp32. Use only the chapter's stated numbers (406/203/102/63 MB, 101.4M params); invent nothing new. Right 40%, a PACKING inset: show one row of int4 quantized values as small integer cells (values 0..15), then show two adjacent cells (an even-column value and an odd-column value) being folded into a single byte — draw a byte as 8 bit-cells split into a low nibble (even) and high nibble (odd), with 'low = even col, high = odd col' labels, matching q_even | (q_odd<<4). Below the inset, a one-line caveat banner: 'smaller in RAM, NOT automatically faster — the reference path dequantizes to fp32 before matmul; integer-native kernels (FBGEMM/QNNPACK, GGUF) are what buy speed.' Theme-safe neutrals, two segment roles distinguishable in both light/dark, all inside viewBox, reading order top-to-bottom on the bars.
new_figures.theme_note: distinguish 'weight bytes' vs 'scale/zp overhead' by pattern or luminance, not by a fixed hue that breaks in dark mode

new_figures.name: gptq-vs-awq-two-philosophies
new_figures.concept: GPTQ corrects quantization error AFTER the fact by redistributing it onto not-yet-quantized columns via the Hessian; AWQ protects salient high-activation channels BEFORE quantizing by rescaling.
new_figures.rationale: 5.2 and 5.3 present the two production upgrades over RTN with dense math (Hessian inverse, salient-channel rescaling). The shared intuition — some weights matter more than others, and there are two opposite strategies (fix-after vs protect-before) to exploit that — is the single takeaway the Interview Corner rests on. A side-by-side diptych makes the contrast click far faster than reading both derivations.
new_figures.placement: 5.3 AWQ: protect the salient channels instead of correcting for them
new_figures.brief: A titled diptych, 'Two ways to beat RTN', over a shared one-line premise: 'RTN treats every weight as equally important; these do not.' LEFT panel — GPTQ 'correct after': draw a weight matrix as a grid of columns. Columns to the left are shaded as 'already quantized (locked to the grid)', one highlighted column is 'quantizing now', columns to the right are 'not yet quantized (still full precision)'. From the current column, draw error arrows fanning RIGHTWARD onto the not-yet-quantized columns, labeled 'spread this column's rounding error onto future columns, weighted by the Hessian H^-1 so the layer's OUTPUT reconstruction stays accurate'. Small note: 'needs calibration activations + a Hessian inverse per layer — accurate but heavier.' RIGHT panel — AWQ 'protect before': draw the same layer as input CHANNELS feeding weight columns, with a small subset (~1 of ~10 shown) marked as 'salient: systematically large activation'. Show a before/after rescale: multiply the salient weight columns UP by s>1 (drawn larger/bolder) and divide the matching activations by s (drawn smaller), with the invariance label 'y = W^T x = (W diag(s))^T (x/s) — output unchanged, but rounding now hurts the salient channels less.' Small note: 'found by a cheap grid search — no backprop, no Hessian.' Bottom strip both panels share: 'both preserve the high-leverage precision a position-blind metric like perplexity would never flag.' Small illustrative counts only; theme-safe neutrals with one accent role for 'salient/current'; everything inside viewBox; clear left/right reading order.
new_figures.theme_note: reserve exactly one accent role for the salient channel / current column so both panels read consistently in light and dark

new_figures.name: honest-eval-four-probes-asymmetry
new_figures.concept: The four measurements probe different skills and lean on different model capacities, producing a characteristic asymmetry — narrow/targeted probes score well, broad-knowledge probes near chance — which is itself the honest finding.
new_figures.rationale: The evaluation half is fully half the chapter and currently has no visual. The key intuition is not any single metric but the RELATIONSHIP among them: perplexity is trustworthy-but-blind, the three probes isolate different skills, and the pattern across them (plus the honest 'cannot do' report) is the deliverable. A single concept map turns four code blocks and a results table into one legible mental model and anchors why cloze-scoring exists at this scale.
new_figures.brief: A concept map with four probe cards arranged along a vertical axis labeled at the bottom 'broad / parametric knowledge' at one end and 'narrow / scaffolded, grading unambiguous' at the other. Cards: (1) HELD-OUT PERPLEXITY — 'predictive fit to held-out web text; cheap to make honest (provably excluded shard); the one trustworthy number — but averages over everything and can stay flat while a capability collapses.' Draw it slightly apart as 'the meter, not a skill test'. (2) ARITHMETIC exact-match — 'reliable reasoning; directly checks whether narrow RLVR stuck; scores well above chance.' (3) TINY MC, CLOZE-SCORED — small inset showing the cloze mechanic: question + each candidate answer appended, sum log p(token) per option, pick the max (not: emit the letter 'A' — instruction-following too weak at 100M); label 'needs broad world knowledge the model never had capacity to store -> sits near a coin flip.' (4) RETRIEVAL-QA exact-match — 'reading comprehension when the answer is handed to it in context; isolates comprehension from parametric memory; scores well.' Use a light vertical position encoding so cards 2 and 4 sit toward the 'narrow, scores high' end and card 3 toward the 'broad, near chance' end, with a short annotation 'the asymmetry IS the finding.' Along the bottom, a banded footer: 'the deliverable is the number PLUS an explicit statement of what it cannot do.' Do NOT print specific percentage scores (the chapter gives only illustrative ranges) — encode relative height/position qualitatively, invent no numbers. Theme-safe, all inside viewBox, top-to-bottom then the footer.
new_figures.theme_note: use position/height for the high-vs-chance signal rather than red/green; keep card fills theme-neutral

summary: This chapter is figure-poor (zero figures) but concept-rich, with two clearly separated halves: honest evaluation and efficient serving. I propose four foundational static figures, no animations (every mechanism here resolves cleanly in a single well-labeled frame). Two priority-1 figures cover the serving half's load-bearing intuitions: the RTN number-line mapping (the mechanism every later quantization idea builds on) and the memory-shrink ladder with int4 nibble-packing and the memory-not-speed caveat (the chapter's headline payoff). Two priority-2 figures cover the conceptual peaks: the GPTQ-vs-AWQ 'two philosophies' diptych (fix-after vs protect-before, which the Interview Corner rests on) and an honest-evaluation concept map showing how the four probes test different skills and why their asymmetry is the finding. No existing figures to audit.
